newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore refiners minimise reforming losses.
newsitem.headline: Singapore refiners minimise reforming losses.

text.p: Singapore refiners are minimising the risk of losses on running secondary reforming units by selling gasoline based on the much higher naphtha price, industry sources said on Friday.
"By selling (the gasoline) naphtha related, we are capitalising on the strength of naphtha from now until the early part of the year," said a light distillates trader at a Singapore refinery.
Traders in Singapore have been offering prompt December lifting cargoes of 95-octane unleaded gasoline at a premium as high as $3.50 a barrel over Singapore spot quotes of naphtha.
They said they could at least lock-in a higher price as the gasoline spot quote was only around $2.50 above naphtha spot quotes.

"But you are still talking about locking in a loss," said a trader at a refinery, referring to the profit potential on reforming. He said the break-even cost for producing gasoline is at least $4 per barrel.

Profits from reforming, the refining process of producing gasoline component reformate and hydrogen from straight-run naphtha, disappeared in the middle of the year when new refining capacity in Thailand and South Korea swung the region's gasoline balance into surplus.
As a result, reformers in Singapore have not been operating at full capacity but at a sufficient capacity to cover their needs for hydrogen.
"You can only sell naphtha-related when it is a seller's market," one trader at a major oil company said, describing the current market as at least balanced with the prompt even tight.

Traders said demand has been strong recently, with November and December cargoes moving from Thailand, Singapore and Yanbu (in Saudi Arabia) to Australia and New Zealand for their summer driving seasons.
In addition, five cargoes or 1.25 million barrels of gasoline were destined for the main regional buyer Taiwan in December.
"But for how long will this last?" questioned a bearish trader.
"Come January, the market may crash," he said, which would mean sellers would lose their advantage.

In addition, supplies in the region are due to rise in December with the return from maintenance of Shell's 35,000 barrel-per-day (bpd) cracker in Singapore and an 80,000 bpd residue catalytic cracker in Balongan in Indonesia.
Traders also expected the new 100,000-bpd Dalian refinery in north China to export up to three 90-octane cargoes of 30,000 tonnes each a month from January.
